A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPLIT, LicketySPLIT, and RESPLIT research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including material moved between the appendix and main text.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, runtime, ablation, scaling, and Rashomon-set experiments in Section 6 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds Blossom comparisons, further CART evaluations, and predictive-multiplicity results.

M1.justification: RESPLIT indexing changes from answering an individual index query through binary search over prefix counts (v1 Algorithm 7) to enumerating trees into a dictionary (v2 Algorithm 9). The principal SPLIT, LicketySPLIT, and RESPLIT tree-generation procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same ten datasets, represented by the nine classification datasets in Table 3 and the additional HIV dataset in Table 4. New comparisons and analyses reuse this coverage; preprocessing and sparsity variations do not introduce new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Blossom is newly evaluated against LicketySPLIT across nine datasets, both when allowed to finish and under approximately matched runtimes (v2 Tables 5–6). The original comparator roster remains. CART corresponds to the earlier scikit-learn Greedy baseline, with additional evaluation settings.

E3.justification: v2 adds full-run and approximately time-matched Blossom protocols, comparisons within specified leaf-count ranges, continuous-versus-binary CART inputs, and runtimes explicitly including binarization. Tables 5–6 select LicketySPLIT configurations by best test loss. The reported lookahead depth for depth-four experiments changes from 1 to 2, and Table 14 introduces a lambda = 0.00001 setting.

E4.justification: New analyses test CART's sensitivity to input binarization (Tables 15–17), behavior with less sparse trees and weak regularization (Tables 13–14), and whether RESPLIT preserves predictive multiplicity beyond variable importance (Section A.14). Existing lookahead, postprocessing, discretization, scaling, and RID analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The original averages and standard errors over three train-test splits remain. v2 adds explicit 95% confidence intervals in Tables 5–6 and 10–17 and specifies five trials for the Blossom comparisons and Table 14. This extends reporting without establishing that the original experiments received additional runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive numerical outcomes for Blossom, CART, training objectives, preprocessing costs, and predictive multiplicity. For example, Table 5 reports Bike runtimes of 158.744 seconds for Blossom versus 1.679 for LicketySPLIT, with test losses of 0.112 versus 0.121. These are new comparisons, not performance gains over v1; Tables 1–4 retain their values.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 4 revises v1 Equation 3 by removing the extra lambda penalty from the subtree-sum alternatives. The greedy-separation proof also revises logarithmic bounds, including O(u log u) to O(u/log u) and O(d_l^2 log^2 d_l) to O(d_l^2/log^2 d_l). The theorem statements and remaining proof framework are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: near-optimal accuracy and sparsity with substantially faster tree optimization, theoretical advantages over greedy and globally optimal approaches, and scalable Rashomon-set approximation.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets prediction-variance results as showing little change in predictive multiplicity under RESPLIT (Section A.14). It also discusses Blossom's accuracy-sparsity tradeoffs and qualifies the practical desirability of non-sparse trees in Table 14. The original mechanism explanations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a first-page repository link for algorithms and experiments. New tables separately document binarization costs and explain their inclusion in SPLIT runtimes. Existing hardware specifications, dataset preparation instructions, and most hyperparameter descriptions are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Demirovic et al. (2023) and positions Blossom's bottom-up anytime search against SPLIT's emphasis on optimizing decisions near the root. It also explicitly describes Murtree as extending Aglin et al. (2020). The remaining cited works are retained.

P1.justification: The motivation previously in v1 Appendix A.2 becomes main-text Section 4, with limited rewriting and corresponding renumbering. v2 also updates the running title and adds acknowledgements, an impact statement, and appendix sections. Most existing prose remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The comparison-frontier figures are redrawn with revised colors, markers, axis ranges, legends, and panel titles. The former appendix heatmap becomes main-text Figure 2. New Figures 20–23 and Tables 5–18 substantially expand the visual presentation, including additional results and reorganized views of retained comparisons.

improvement.justification: v1 already provides extensive empirical and technical support. v2 strengthens it with preprocessing-cost accounting, CART representation controls, predictive-multiplicity checks, confidence intervals, and code-access information. These are useful incremental gains. The new Blossom comparisons select LicketySPLIT configurations by test loss, which limits the strength of their generalization evidence.
